Natural Order, Physiocracy and Reform
1. Aims of the lecture
To demonstrate the emergence in France during the first half of the eighteenth century of
arguments over trade and regulation in relation to issues of food supply that moved away from
comparisons of the “strength of a nation” and introduced arguments about the existence of a
“natural order” in economic life.
To outline the early history of physiocracy through discussion of Quesnay’s Tableau
 and the associated , and show how these economic principlesÉconomique Maximes
transformed in the course of the 1760s into a more general argument concerning natural order
and good government.
To demonstrate that arguments about “free trade” in the early eighteenth century were related
primarily to grain markets, but that by the 1780s these had transformed into general arguments
about economic deregulation.
To show that the criticisms of the “physiocratic System” made at the time were uniform, limited
and general, that its direct influence quickly waned, but that Quesnay’s  in the 1860sTableau
became an inspiration for Marx, and thence indirectly for both Soviet planning and early
input–output models of the economy.

4. Lecture summary
The context
The oeconomists of the absolutist state, the so-called Mercantilists, regarded the
economic life of peoples as the product of human government, a life whose purpose was
attained by decree. The Physiocrats and Adam Smith, by contrast, claimed that the
human world was governed by natural laws as immutable as those which ruled the world
of plants and minerals; hence they considered all such government regulations to be
disadvantageous restraints imposed upon the healthy development of economic life
according to its own natural laws. Against the mercantilist system of prohibition and
protection they set the principle of free trade; against the established orders of guilds and
industrial monopolies they set free competition; against the remnants of the medieval
agrarian constitution they set the necessity of completely free and partible landed
property; against the system of commercial police they set that of unconditional
commercial freedom.

Out of this Enlightenment confrontation there emerged Political Economy as a new
science of the natural laws of human exchange, which was to achieve for human society
something similar to that which Physics and Chemistry had accomplished for the entire
material world.1
Bruno Hildebrand’s characterization of the shift in thinking that took place in mid-eighteenth-
century France follows Adam Smith’s basic critique of regulation that put into general circulation
the idea of “mercantilism”, which, as suggested in our introduction, is a seriously flawed approach
to any modern understanding of the diversity of economic writing in the seventeenth and early
eighteenth centuries. It is flawed because it places the emphasis on “free trade” versus
“regulation”, obscuring the fact that free markets are also regulated markets. It is a question of
different regimes of regulation, not of the presence or absence of regulation; economic and
political liberty are predicated upon a robust state, not on its absence. Instead, the development of
early modern economic literature is better approached in terms of a gradual shift from an empirical
evaluation of existing states and their economies to a more abstract version of the same basic
evaluation, but now organized in terms of general categories such as wealth, labour, growth and
distribution. It is for this reason that Adam Smith’s Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations
should be treated as a synthesis of these new arguments developed in the course of the preceding
60 or 70 years, and not primarily as the baseline for a hitherto non-existent political economy.
All the same, Hildebrand does here capture the sense of novelty in physiocratic argument:
that human activity was governed by natural laws, rendering active government direction of this
activity redundant at best and harmful at worst. Furthermore, in the mid-eighteenth century the
physiocrats identified agricultural production as the source of wealth, and so their argument about
the natural laws of human conduct was doubled by the idea that this conduct was most profitably
exercised in respect of the natural world. By contrast, they argued that activity devoted to
manufacture was “sterile”, producing at most its own subsistence, and not capable of supporting
any but those directly engaged in manufacturing occupations. As we shall see, this assessment of
manufacturing and agricultural activity came in for a great deal of criticism, but this critique
overlooked the fact that the “sterility” of manufacture was the corollary of treating the natural
world as the unique space in which the activity of humans produced more than the cost of their
subsistence – a natural surplus.
It should already be apparent that these kinds of arguments have moved away from the
empirical arguments of the seventeenth century into a new kind of discourse that sought, by using
abstract reasoning, to identify the sources of wealth and the effects of its circulation. Following on
from Boisguilbert’s idea of an emergent balance between a buyer and a seller united by their self-
interest and by the mutual assumption that one would buy what the other was selling, economic
argument in France shifted from a discussion of the type of economic activities that should be
promoted to an evaluation of the more abstract sources of wealth. When in 1734 Jean-François
Melon published his , this work was unusual for the way that itEssai politique sur le commerce
began with a chapter entitled “Principes”, an abstract argument about exchange between three
islands, each with the same number of inhabitants and producing only one good: grain or wool or
wine ( ). The same number of workers were engaged in production on each island and theboissons
product was sufficient for the three islands; trade in these products therefore arose, each island

The work was soon translated into English, and the translator of the Dublin edition remarked
in his preface:
The Principles laid down by our Author will hold universally true in all Countries. It is
certain that the Improvement of Agriculture, and other necessary and useful Industries;
the Encrease of Inhabitants; and the procuring to the Society, a sufficient Quantity of the
common Measure of Permutations, that is to say, Money and its representations, are the

In fact, another Irishman, Richard Cantillon, had by the 1730s already drafted a treatise that would
not only “hold universally true” but that considered the source of wealth, the genesis of markets,
the value of land and of labour, the circulation of goods, the factors governing the rise and fall of
population, the quantity of money, and the causes of fluctuation in interest rates, and which
concluded with a discussion of foreign trade. While Essai sur la nature du commerce en général
was first published in French in 1755, it appears to have been written – perhaps in English,
perhaps in French – during the period 1728–30: before Melon’s essay. Cantillon’s essay opens
with a clear statement of the nature of wealth: “Land is the source or the matter from which wealth
is derived; labor is the form that produces it, and wealth is itself nothing other than food,
commodities, and the comforts of life.”  Fifty years later, describing the “nature” of the “wealth of4
a nation”, Adam Smith opened with a version of the same affirmation:
The annual labour of every nation is the fund which originally supplies it with all the
necessaries and conveniences of life which it annually consumes and which consist
always, either in the immediate produce of that labour, or in what is purchased with the
produce from other nations.5
Cantillon’s text marked a turning point in the assessment of national wealth, economic activity and
trade, from an empirical appraisal of how a particular nation might best configure its resources to
produce power and plenty, to a theoretical assessment of the sources of power and plenty in any
nation. Moreover, the  appeared at the beginning of a sudden boom in economic writing thatEssai
would last until 1789: while 85 books were published in France on economic topics during the
decade 1740–9, in 1750–59 the total shot up to 349, continuing to increase until it reached 1,284 in
1780–89.  The less than straightforward publishing history of Cantillon’s book provides us with a6
link back to arguments over economic regulation and reform in mid-century France that
subsequently became increasingly intense.

Food supply, trade and regulation
For eighteenth-century France, grain was a staple product produced domestically, forming the
basic foodstuff for the majority of the country’s population. Grain  was the system by whichpolice
the price of grain was regulated to assure that grain flowed from producer to consumer, deploying
price ceilings, subsidies, the storage of grain or its distribution, together with straight coercion in
some cases. These direct measures ensured that markets cleared but did not empty: “free trade”
here meant the free movement of grain from the countryside to the city, and only secondarily the
freedom for owners of grain to sell how, where and when they wished. There was a market in
grain that looked as though it operated freely according to the play of demand and supply but that
was in fact an ongoing work in progress on the part of local administrations.14
The , first sketched by François Quesnay (1694–1774) in 1758,Tableau Économique
provided a representation of the basic relationships of production and consumption that drew on
the principles outlined by Cantillon and others, in so doing lending emphasis to a fundamental
feature of a grain-based economy: that there is an annual production cycle, the summer harvest
providing both food for consumption over the subsequent year and seed to be sown for the new
crop. Yields were low by present-day standards, and a substantial amount of any one harvest had
to be set aside for sowing the following spring. Grain was therefore distributed through time and
space: once harvested, grain had to be transported to its consumers and sufficient quantities had to
be stored to cover consumption until the next harvest set the cycle off all over again. Local and
regional markets, together with the activities of corn merchants, were important in the formation
of grain prices that would effect this dual distribution, through space and through time.
The yield fluctuated from year to year: as adverse weather conditions spoiled sown crops or
limited the growing season; or as ideal growing conditions contributed to bumper harvests. Since
the domestic demand for grain was relatively inelastic, and there was only limited trade in grain
across frontiers, the price fluctuations that resulted from variations in the annual harvest led to
constant redistribution between domestic consumers and producers. If the harvest was poor, then
prices rose, producers tended to do well, and consumers suffered; conversely, if the harvest was
good, prices fell, consumers benefited, and farming profits were reduced. Hence in times of dearth
the distribution of grain could become a political issue: the rise in prices squeezing the poor, and
the physical movement of grain triggering unrest.
Grain security was a constant political problem; and the conventional wisdom was that the
food supply was best secured by preventing any export. The idea that one country might become
dependent on another through the regular import of grain trumped arguments that production
could be permanently expanded and the food supply secured more readily if it were easier to trade
in grain between nations. According to the former view, while it was advantageous to export any
surplus that might arise, permitting imports could well undermine local production. It was in this
context that the first arguments about “free trade” emerged: Boisguilbert had written of “freedom
of trade in grain” but by this he meant the freedom to export, not to import. He argued that
Colbert, by preventing the export of a grain surplus, lowered prices at home, and this favoured

The background to the Tableau Économique
Appended to “Grains” was the first version of Quesnay’s “Maxims of Economic Government”,
which articulates many of the principles that the  would illustrate. The firstTableau Économique
four of these were as follows:18
Human industry does not multiply wealth.19
Human industry contributes [through foreign trade] to population and the growth of wealth.
Human industry that occupies men to the prejudice of the cultivation of property is harmful to
the population and to the growth of wealth.
The wealth of cultivators brings about the wealth of cultivation.
There were 14 maxims in all, the last of them relating to the balance of trade between nations; but
they all presupposed the agrarian origin of wealth and the advantages of free trade in the products
of agriculture and industry.
In 1756 Mirabeau had published , which usedL’ami des hommes ou Traité de la population
the idea of “population” to develop an argument about the centrality of agriculture to the creation
of wealth and criticized Melon’s positive view of luxury, stating that “Luxury is the abuse of
wealth”.  Subsequently, Quesnay persuaded Mirabeau that a large population was not the cause20
of wealth but its effect, and that therefore the proper object of analysis was not population but
wealth. The sixth part of Mirabeau’s  in 1760 advocated this new viewpoint,L’ami des hommes
and was devoted to an exposition of the :Tableau Économique
The  was originally conceived as a printing exercise undertaken purely as a diversion:Tableau
it is not, as in the English translation of 1758, an “economical table”, a means for the calculation
of product and its distribution, but more an “economic picture”, a general representation of
economic relationships. Nevertheless, in its graphic representation it encapsulates most of the
characteristics later associated with physiocratic thinking.
There is an annual cycle that unites through their incomes and expenditures the three classes of
society: farmers, landowners and manufacturers.
Agriculture is the unique source of value, which as it circulates between the classes is gradually
dissipated.
Following each annual harvest, agricultural products would be exchanged for manufactured
goods, so that the “sterile class” of artisans and manufacturers gained food and wine, while
the “productive class” received in turn manufactured goods.
Landowners, who receive the entire net product of the land as rent, distribute the 600 livres of
net produce from agriculture equally between the productive and sterile classes: to the
agricultural sector as purchases of food and wine and to “sterile expenditures” for the
manufacturers of luxury goods. The latter then in turn spend half of their income on food and
wine and the other half on manufactured goods.
And so on through the year, until the entire system runs down to nothing and the next harvest
starts the sequence once more.

Circulation within the kingdom should be free of the impediment that special taxes and duties

Economic government should observe these natural laws; not only should it permit the free

Luxury goods could therefore be obtained from overseas producers in exchange for the net

its duties.
“Book V. Of the Revenue of the Sovereign or Commonwealth” (pp. 689–947)
Book V is by far the longest of the five books but consists of only three chapters: the expenditures
of the sovereign, sources of revenue, and public debt.
The income of the sovereign has two sources: from land or property belonging to the
sovereign, and from the people. The first is dealt with very quickly, before attention is turned to
taxation. Smith laid down four enduring principles: that the tax levied upon the person be
proportionate to their ability to pay; that tax due be certain as to timing and manner of payment,
and the amount payable; that taxes be levied in a time and manner suited to the contributor; and
that taxes be as low as is possible (V.ii.b.3–6). There then follows an exhaustive review of forms
of taxation in the light of these principles.
The third chapter opens with a discussion of the dispositions to save and to spend that draws
upon the arguments of , first suggesting that a sovereign is no lessTheory of Moral Sentiments
distracted by frivolities and trinkets than his subjects, so that at best “his ordinary expence
becomes equal to his ordinary revenue” (V.iii.3). The failure to set anything aside for defence
means that when war looms debts are contracted. The ability of the sovereign to borrow presumes
that the lenders have confidence in the state, and indeed, “commerce and manufactures can seldom
flourish long in any state which does not enjoy a regular administration of justice, in which the
people do not feel themselves secure in the possession of their property, in which the faith of
contracts is not supported by law” (V.iii.7). Hence in such a state merchants and manufacturers
will be prepared to lend to the state, since this does not impair their ability to carry on their own
business; indeed, they further their business by lending money at interest to the state.
